exact_task.problem:
Let X be a connected compact reduced locally irreducible (unibranch) complex space of pure complex dimension n, with a smooth Hermitian background h in the local-embedding sense. This means that near every point an embedding into an open set of complex Euclidean space realizes h as the restriction of a smooth strictly positive ambient (1,1)-form. The background is not assumed closed. Use dd^c=(i/(2 pi))partial barpartial. Potentials are genuine quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives, locally defined by holomorphic disk tests and canonical upper values. On each holomorphic disk f into X, choose a local smooth real potential p_f with dd^c p_f=f* h; then u composed with f plus p_f is genuine subharmonic or identically minus infinity. A disk contained in a pole set is allowed to have identically-minus-infinity restriction and is not assigned a distributional derivative. The potential u itself is not identically minus infinity on X. Arbitrary null-set modifications are excluded. On a resolution pi:Y->X the extended non-pluripolar measure is computed from pi*h+dd^c(pi*u) upstairs and pushed forward; any claimed equation and singularity class must be independent of common refinements. Ordinary type of a reference psi means u<=psi+C and psi<=u+C for a finite constant C, with genuine canonical extended values, so common poles are interpreted without subtracting minus infinity from minus infinity. For finite positive non-pluripolar Borel data nu, the desired normalized equations have form MA_ext_h(u)=c nu, c>0, sup_X u=0, in a specified genuine singularity type.

notes.detailedSummary: Let X be a compact reduced locally irreducible curve whose normalization π:E=C/Λ→X is finite and bijective, hence a homeomorphism, and is biholomorphic outside finitely many points. Write β=π*h=bβ0, where β0 is normalized flat area, b is smooth nonnegative, and H=∫β>0. Choose distinct q_j∈E and weights a_j>0 with A=Σa_j<H. A periodic Green function G with dd^cG=δ0−β0 and G=log|z|²+smooth is constructed by a cutoff and Fourier series. Define Φ=G*((H−b)β0), Ψ=Φ+Σa_jG(·−q_j), and ψ=Ψ∘π^{-1}. This is a genuine h-potential with logarithmic pole type; β+dd^cΨ=(H−A)β0+Σa_jδq_j. For f≥0 in L^p(E,β0), p>1, F=∫f>0, and ν=π_*(fβ0), the equation has c=(H−A)/F and solution U=Ψ+G*((cf−(H−A))β0), descended and normalized by subtracting its supremum. Its residual relative to ψ is continuous, the potential is real-continuous off the poles and continuous into R∪{−∞} at the poles. Every genuine potential in the ordinary type has extended non-pluripolar mass H−A. Any solution in the entire ordinary type has the same pole atoms and hence the same c; the difference of pullbacks is distributionally harmonic and therefore constant. Descent is proved by holomorphic lifting of all disks and the singleton-fiber property. All resolutions and common refinements are biholomorphic to E. The theorem is deliberately scoped to dimension one and finite logarithmic types, not to arbitrary dimensions or singularities.
notes.text:
THEOREM: AN ELEMENTARY NONNORMAL, NON-CONE SUFFICIENT-CONDITION FAMILY

This is a scoped dimension-one result. Its geometric hypotheses are explicit and do not include existence, uniqueness, or continuity of the desired solution.

Geometric hypotheses:
(1) X is a connected compact reduced complex curve, locally irreducible, and there is a finite bijective normalization map π:E→X, where E=C/Λ is a complex torus. The map is biholomorphic away from a finite set. (Equivalently, the normalization of the unibranch curve is this torus.)
(2) h is any smooth Hermitian background in the local-embedding sense in the question. No closed ambient extension is required.

Let dA be flat Euclidean area on E, let V=∫E dA, and put β0=dA/V, so ∫Eβ0=1. The smooth pullback β=π*h can be written β=bβ0 with b smooth and nonnegative. It is positive on the inverse image of X_reg, but it is NOT assumed positive everywhere. In particular, it can vanish at a cusp. Put H=∫Eβ=∫E bβ0>0. In real dimension two every smooth 2-form is closed; this is the reason the argument works for arbitrary h in this dimension.

Singularity hypotheses and the actual class:
Choose distinct points q_1,...,q_k of E and positive numbers a_1,...,a_k, with A=Σ_j a_j<H. The empty list, A=0, is allowed. The reference ψ below is a genuine h-potential. The specified class consists of ALL genuine h-potentials w with w≤ψ+C and ψ≤w+C for some finite C, interpreted by these inequalities at common −∞ values. No smoothness or continuity of w is assumed.

Measure hypotheses:
Choose a nonnegative f∈L^p(E,β0) for a finite p>1, with F=∫E fβ0>0. The prescribed measure is ν=π_*(fβ0). This is finite and non-pluripolar. The condition is on the normalization-side density, not on a density with respect to the possibly degenerating h-volume on X.

Conclusions:
Every potential in the specified class has finite extended non-pluripolar mass M=H−A. There is a solution of
 MA_ext,h(u)=cν,   sup_X u=0,
with c=M/F>0, in the specified ordinary type. It is unique among all genuine potentials in that type, even if a competing solution is initially rough and has its own unknown positive proportionality constant. Unnormalized solutions differ by constants, with equality of canonical extended values at common poles. The solution is continuous as a real function away from its finite pole set, and it is continuous into R∪{−∞}, with the order topology, at its poles. Its residual relative to the specified reference, initially defined away from the poles, extends to a continuous real-valued function on all of X. No subtraction of −∞ from −∞ is used. The equation, class, and continuity statements are independent of resolutions and common refinements.

Here is a complete elementary construction and proof.

1. Normalization of dd^c and a periodic Green function.
In a flat coordinate z=x+iy,
 dd^c v=(Δv/(4π)) dA.
Indeed, ∂bar∂ has the usual scalar coefficient Δ/4 and i dz∧dbar z=2dA. The divergence theorem gives Δ log|z|²=4πδ0, hence, with exactly the normalization in the question,
 dd^c log|z|²=δ0.
There is no factor 2 missing in the pole weights below.

We construct, rather than invoke an elliptic existence theorem, a real distribution G on E with
 dd^c G=δ0−β0,   ∫E Gβ0=0,
and G(z)=log|z|²+smooth near 0, smooth elsewhere. Choose a smooth cutoff supported in a small coordinate disk, equal to 1 near 0, and let L be the cutoff times log|z|², extended by zero. Then
 dd^c L=δ0+qβ0,
where q is smooth and ∫qβ0=−1: pair this distributional equality with the constant function 1. Thus q+1 has mean zero. If ξ ranges over the dual lattice and −Δ e_ξ=λ_ξe_ξ, λ_ξ>0 for ξ≠0, solve
 dd^c S=−(q+1)β0
by the Fourier coefficients S_ξ=(4π/V)(q+1)_ξ/λ_ξ, ξ≠0. Repeated integration by parts shows the coefficients of q+1 decay faster than every power, so this series and every derivative converge uniformly. Set G=L+S and subtract its mean. This proves all the claimed properties. In particular G∈L^r(E,β0) for every finite r, because a logarithm has this integrability.

For r∈L^p and the group convolution K=G*(rβ0), distributional differentiation gives
 dd^c K=(r−∫E rβ0)β0.
The calculation follows directly by pairing with a smooth test function and using dd^c_zG(z−t)=δ_t−β0. Fubini is legitimate since G is integrable and the test-function convolution is smooth. Smooth mean-zero r gives smooth K, either from the Fourier construction or by multiplying the rapidly decaying Fourier coefficients.

For r∈L^p, p>1, K is continuous and bounded. With p'=p/(p−1), Hölder gives
 |K(z+s)−K(z)|≤||r||_p ||G(·+s)−G||_{p'}.
Translations are continuous in L^{p'}: approximate G in that norm by smooth functions and use their uniform translation continuity. Also ||K||_∞≤||G||_{p'}||r||_p. These observations independently give the precise continuity assertion needed here; no continuity theorem on singular spaces is invoked.

2. Explicit genuine reference and solution upstairs.
Define the smooth function
 Φ=G*((H−b)β0).
The density has mean zero, and
 dd^cΦ=(H−b)β0.
Define the canonical extended-valued function
 Ψ(z)=Φ(z)+Σ_j a_jG(z−q_j).
It is finite and smooth away from Q={q_j}, equals −∞ at each q_j, and near q_j has the form a_j log|ζ|² plus a smooth function. Directly,
 β+dd^cΨ=Mβ0+Σ_j a_jδ_{q_j},   M=H−A>0.
Thus Ψ is genuinely β-subharmonic; its local sums with smooth primitives of β are genuine subharmonic representatives. A smooth local primitive exists by solving the scalar smooth Laplace equation in a coordinate disk, for example by convolving a compactly supported smooth extension of its density with log|z|². Positivity of the displayed measure gives subharmonicity by local smoothing; the logarithmic and smooth expressions fix the canonical upper values.

Set c=M/F and r=cf−M, which has mean zero. Put
 v=G*(rβ0),   U=Ψ+v.
The preceding estimates make v a bounded continuous real function. Moreover
 β+dd^c U=cfβ0+Σ_j a_jδ_{q_j}.
It is a positive measure, so U is genuinely β-subharmonic with its canonical values, and U is in the ordinary type of Ψ. It tends to −∞ at Q. Its supremum S is finite: it is upper semicontinuous on the compact torus, not identically −∞, and its positive singularities are bounded above. Subtract S for normalization.

3. Descent is proved, not assumed.
A finite bijective proper map between the present Hausdorff compact spaces is a homeomorphism. Thus the only possible descended functions are ψ=Ψ∘π^{-1} and u=(U−S)∘π^{-1}; their fibers are singleton fibers and their canonical values agree exactly, including the value −∞ at a pole.

Every holomorphic disk f:D→X has a holomorphic lift F:D→E. For a nonconstant disk, f^{-1}(X_sing) is discrete. On its complement the lift is holomorphic because π is biholomorphic there. The continuous lift π^{-1}∘f stays in a bounded coordinate neighborhood at each omitted point; the usual one-variable removable-singularity argument for its coordinate function therefore extends it holomorphically. Constant disks have constant lifts. A nonconstant disk cannot have image in the finite singular set.

On a sufficiently small disk take a local smooth primitive p of β on the image of F. Then p∘F is a smooth potential for f*h, since F*β=f*h. The function
 (u∘f)+(p∘F)=(U−S+p)∘F
is subharmonic, or identically −∞, by holomorphic composition of a subharmonic function. This composition property follows, for example, by decreasing smooth subharmonic regularizations and the smooth chain rule Δ(v∘F)=|F'|²(Δv)∘F. Any other smooth primitive for f*h differs by a harmonic function. Therefore the exact disk tests in the question hold. A constant disk in a pole has identically −∞ restriction; no distributional derivative is assigned to that restriction. If a nonconstant lifted disk meets q_j with order m, the local logarithmic coefficient is m a_j, as follows from log|ζ(F(t))|²=m log|t|²+smooth. This also records the disk ramification factor explicitly.

The homeomorphism and the explicit logarithmic behavior prove the canonical upper-value statements downstairs. They also prove real continuity off π(Q) and extended continuity to −∞ at π(Q). The residual v−S descends to a continuous REAL function on all of X. This function, and not an undefined subtraction at the poles, is the asserted residual.

4. Non-pluripolar measure and finite mass of the entire type.
In dimension one, for a β-subharmonic function W which is locally bounded away from Q and has value −∞ precisely at Q, put T_W=β+dd^cW. The non-pluripolar measure is
 <β+dd^cW>=1_{E\Q}T_W.
This follows directly from the truncation definition: on each relatively compact set avoiding Q a sufficiently low truncation equals W, so the linear product is T_W; the pole set is removed by the indicator in that definition. No higher-dimensional continuity or comparison theorem is used.

For any genuine downstairs w in the ordinary type, W=w∘π is locally β-subharmonic by applying the disk tests to normalization coordinate disks. The type inequalities imply that W is finite and locally bounded on E\Q and, near q_j,
 W=a_j log|ζ|²+O(1),
with W(q_j)=−∞. It is locally integrable and T_W is a positive distribution, hence a positive Radon measure. Its total mass is H, since the distribution dd^cW pairs to zero with 1 on the compact torus.

We verify the atom weights, without an assumption about a competing solution's regularity. If s=W+p is subharmonic near q_j, where dd^cp=β, its circular mean m(t) satisfies, for almost every t,
 m'(t)=2 T_W(B_t)/t.
This is the divergence theorem for smooth approximants; local convergence of their Laplacians gives the distributional version. If τ=T_W({q_j}), then T_W(B_t)→τ and integrating the identity shows
 lim_{t→0} m(t)/log t²=τ.
But W=a_j log|ζ|²+O(1), and p is smooth, so the same limit is a_j. Consequently T_W({q_j})=a_j. The coefficient is invariant under a change of normalization coordinate, since the difference of the two logarithms is smooth. It follows that EVERY genuine potential in the entire ordinary type has
 ∫E<β+dd^cW>=H−Σ_j a_j=M<∞.

For the constructed solution, removal of these atoms gives <β+dd^cU>=cfβ0. Hence, with the original normalization unchanged,
 MA_ext,h(u)=π_*(cfβ0)=cν,
and its total mass is cν(X)=cF=M.

The measure ν is non-pluripolar. A nontrivial local quasi-subharmonic representative pulls back to a nontrivial local quasi-subharmonic function on E; its −∞ set has flat area zero, because such a function is locally integrable. Thus local pluripolar sets have zero β0-area and zero fβ0-measure. The homeomorphism transfers this fact to ν on X.

5. Uniqueness in the ENTIRE ordinary class.
Let w be any genuine potential in the specified class satisfying MA_ext,h(w)=dν for some d>0. Its extended mass is M, so dF=M and d=c. Alternatively this follows from the atom calculation and total distributional mass H. Since π is a Borel homeomorphism, the equation implies
 T_W=cfβ0+Σ_j a_jδ_{q_j}=T_U.
Thus dd^c(W−U)=0 as distributions on E. The difference is an L^1 distribution; all its nonzero Fourier coefficients vanish by the flat Laplacian equation. It is therefore a constant distribution. The corresponding local subharmonic representatives agree everywhere, not merely almost everywhere: a genuine subharmonic value is the limit of its shrinking disk averages, so its almost-everywhere class determines its canonical values. Hence W=U+K with genuine extended values; in particular both sides are −∞ at Q. The same equality holds downstairs. A supremum normalization fixes K. This proves uniqueness among rough potentials too, rather than only among the explicitly constructed solutions.

6. Resolution independence and the precise measure transformation.
Any resolution ρ:Y→X in dimension one factors holomorphically through E: the continuous map π^{-1}∘ρ is holomorphic by the same local disk lifting/removability argument. The resulting map r:Y→E is a nonconstant proper degree-one map of smooth compact curves. Fibers are finite and the sum of local multiplicities is the degree; degree one makes every local multiplicity one and every fiber a singleton. Thus r is biholomorphic. The same applies to every common refinement. There are no additional exceptional-fiber values or measure terms to lose. Consequently both the class and the computed measure are unchanged on all such resolutions and refinements.

The normalization map in this theorem has generic degree ONE; its possible vanishing differential at a cusp does not change that degree. The formula ν=π_*(fβ0) has no extra degree factor. On X_reg, if β=bβ0, then ν has density (f/b)∘π^{-1} relative to h. Here b contains exactly the derivative/Jacobian factor of the pulled-back h. At singular points this density formula is not used; both fβ0 and its pushforward assign those finitely many points zero mass. The pullback β was only assumed semipositive, and its degeneration was explicitly compensated by Φ in the construction, rather than silently discarded.

Scope and source audit: the theorem requires n=1, torus normalization, finite logarithmic ordinary type, A<H, and the stated L^p condition. It does not address arbitrary higher-dimensional unibranch singularities or arbitrary singularity types. No external Monge–Ampère existence/uniqueness/continuity theorem, uniformization theorem, or log-terminal result is invoked. The solvability and continuity arguments are the explicit cutoff/Fourier/convolution arguments above; the uniqueness argument is linear distribution theory. The one-dimensional non-pluripolar computation is the direct truncation computation. The next note constructs and checks a compact non-cone example satisfying all the geometric hypotheses.

reconstruction.statement:
Dimension-one sufficient-condition theorem. Use dd^c=(i/(2π))∂∂̄. Let X be a connected compact reduced locally irreducible complex curve, and suppose its normalization π:E→X is finite and bijective, where E=ℂ/Λ is a complex torus. Assume π is biholomorphic away from a finite set. Let h be any smooth Hermitian background in the local-embedding sense: locally, h is the restriction of a smooth strictly positive ambient (1,1)-form. No closed ambient extension is required.

A genuine h-potential means a function not identically −∞ on X, with canonical upper values, satisfying the following disk tests: on every holomorphic disk γ into X, locally choose a smooth real p_γ with dd^c p_γ=γ*h; then w∘γ+p_γ is genuinely subharmonic or identically −∞. A disk contained in a pole set may have identically −∞ restriction, to which no distributional derivative is assigned. Arbitrary null-set modifications are not allowed.

Let dA be flat Euclidean area on E, V=∫_E dA, and β₀=dA/V. Write β=π*h=bβ₀. Then b is smooth and nonnegative, β is positive on π⁻¹(X_reg), and H=∫_E β=∫_E bβ₀>0. Positivity of β everywhere is not assumed; β can vanish at a cusp. The smooth 2-form β is closed.

There exists a real mean-zero periodic Green function G on E satisfying
 dd^cG=δ₀−β₀,   ∫_E Gβ₀=0,
with G smooth on E∖{0} and G(z)=log|z|² plus a smooth function near 0, with canonical value G(0)=−∞. It belongs to L^r(E,β₀) for every finite r>0. The normalization is
 dd^c v=(Δv/(4π))dA,   dd^c log|z|²=δ₀.
For any finite p>1 and real r∈L^p(E,β₀), define
 K(z)=G*(rβ₀)(z)=∫_E G(z−t)r(t)β₀(t).
Then K is bounded and continuous and
 dd^cK=(r−∫_E rβ₀)β₀.
If r is smooth and has mean zero, K is smooth. With p′=p/(p−1),
 ||K||_∞≤||G||_{p′}||r||_p,
 |K(z+s)−K(z)|≤||r||_p ||G(·+s)−G||_{p′}
for z,s∈E.

Choose any finite list of distinct points q₁,…,q_k∈E and positive real weights a₁,…,a_k with A=Σ_j a_j<H. The empty list, with A=0, is allowed. Put Q={q₁,…,q_k} and M=H−A>0. Define
 Φ=G*((H−b)β₀),
 Ψ(z)=Φ(z)+Σ_j a_jG(z−q_j).
Then Φ is smooth, dd^cΦ=(H−b)β₀, and
 β+dd^cΨ=Mβ₀+Σ_j a_jδ_{q_j}.
The function Ψ is a genuine β-subharmonic potential, smooth and finite on E∖Q, with canonical value −∞ at every q_j. In a normalization coordinate ζ centered at q_j, Ψ=a_j log|ζ|² plus a smooth function.

The map π is a homeomorphism with singleton fibers. The descended reference ψ=Ψ∘π⁻¹ is a genuine h-potential. Specify its entire ordinary singularity class by
 C_ψ={w: w is a genuine h-potential and there is a finite C with w≤ψ+C and ψ≤w+C on X}.
These inequalities use canonical extended values, including common values −∞; no subtraction of −∞ from −∞ is involved. No smoothness or continuity is imposed on members of C_ψ.

For every w∈C_ψ, W=w∘π is a genuine β-subharmonic potential, locally bounded on E∖Q, with W(q_j)=−∞ and W=a_j log|ζ|²+O(1) near q_j. The distribution
 T_W=β+dd^cW
is a positive Radon measure satisfying
 T_W(E)=H,   T_W({q_j})=a_j.
Its non-pluripolar measure is
 ⟨β+dd^cW⟩=1_{E∖Q}T_W,
and its extended non-pluripolar measure downstairs is
 MA_ext,h(w)=π_*⟨β+dd^cW⟩.
Every member of C_ψ consequently has finite extended non-pluripolar mass exactly M.

Let f≥0 belong to L^p(E,β₀) for a finite p>1, and assume F=∫_E fβ₀>0. Prescribe ν=π_*(fβ₀). This is a finite positive non-pluripolar Borel measure. The density condition is on E with respect to β₀, not with respect to the possibly degenerating h-volume downstairs. Define
 c=M/F,   r=cf−M,
 v=G*(rβ₀),   U=Ψ+v,
 S=sup_E U,   u=(U−S)∘π⁻¹.
Here r has mean zero, v is bounded and continuous, S is finite, and U is a genuine β-subharmonic potential in the ordinary type of Ψ. The normalized descended potential u belongs to C_ψ and satisfies
 β+dd^cU=cfβ₀+Σ_j a_jδ_{q_j},
 ⟨β+dd^cU⟩=cfβ₀,
 MA_ext,h(u)=cν,   sup_X u=0,
 cν(X)=M.

Uniqueness holds in the entire specified genuine class: if w∈C_ψ and MA_ext,h(w)=dν for any d>0, then d=c and w=u+K for a real constant K, with equality of canonical extended values, including the common poles. Thus the supremum-zero solution is unique, even among initially rough competitors and even when their positive proportionality constant is initially unspecified.

The solution u is continuous as a real-valued function on X∖π(Q). At every point of π(Q), u tends to −∞ and is continuous into ℝ∪{−∞} with the order topology. The residual u−ψ, initially defined only on X∖π(Q), extends to the continuous real-valued function (v−S)∘π⁻¹ on all of X. This is an extension of the off-pole residual, not a subtraction of common infinite values. These same regularity conclusions hold for every solution in C_ψ, up to its additive constant.

Every holomorphic disk γ:D→X has a unique holomorphic lift F:D→E with π∘F=γ, including constant disks. If a nonconstant lifted disk meets q_j at t₀ with local order m, its logarithmic coefficient for ψ∘γ and u∘γ is m a_j; equivalently, for a coordinate ζ centered at q_j,
 log|ζ(F(t))|²=m log|t−t₀|² plus a smooth function near t₀.
Constant disks in the pole set retain the identically −∞ restriction without a distributional derivative. The descended potentials satisfy the stipulated disk tests and canonical upper-value requirements.

Every resolution ρ:Y→X factors as ρ=π∘r with r:Y→E biholomorphic. The same holds for every smooth common refinement. Consequently the equation, ordinary singularity class, extended non-pluripolar product, and continuity statements are independent of resolutions and common refinements, with no additional exceptional-fiber values or measure terms.

The normalization π has generic degree one, including when its differential vanishes at a cusp. The measure transformation is precisely ν=π_*(fβ₀), with no additional degree factor. On X_reg,
 ν=((f/b)∘π⁻¹)h,
where b is the full coefficient of the pulled-back background, including its differential/Jacobian contribution. This regular-locus density formula is not used at singular points; fβ₀ and its pushforward assign the finite singular set zero mass. The conclusions are scoped to dimension one, torus normalization, the finite logarithmic ordinary types with A<H, and the stated normalization-side L^p data.
reconstruction.proof:
We prove the statement in dimension one, including uniqueness for the whole stated class. No external Monge–Ampère solvability or continuity theorem is used.

1. Geometry, local potentials, and lifting disks.
A continuous bijection from the compact space E to the Hausdorff space X is a homeomorphism. Thus π has a continuous inverse. Pulling back a local smooth ambient representative of h shows that β=π*h is a smooth nonnegative real 2-form on E. Where π is biholomorphic onto X_reg it is strictly positive. Consequently β=bβ₀ with b smooth and nonnegative, and H=∫bβ₀>0. A 2-form on a real surface is closed; this says nothing about closedness of an ambient extension of h. In particular, we have not asserted strict positivity of β at points over X_sing.

Every nonconstant disk γ:D→X has a holomorphic lift. Indeed, let F=π⁻¹∘γ, initially a continuous map. Away from the inverse image of the finite singular set it is holomorphic. For a nonconstant disk that inverse image is discrete: in a local embedding, the inverse image of a specified point is the common zero set of holomorphic coordinate differences, and at least one of these differences is not identically zero. Near each exceptional disk parameter, continuity places F in a coordinate chart of E. Its coordinate is holomorphic on the punctured disk and bounded there, so its Laurent expansion has no negative terms and it extends holomorphically. This extension agrees with F by continuity. Constant disks have the unique constant lift. Uniqueness in both cases follows from injectivity of π.

For clarity, smooth local potentials for β require no positivity assumption beyond the one already stated. In a coordinate disk write β=ρ dA. Extend ρ smoothly with compact support to the plane. The convolution of this extension with log|z|² is smooth and has dd^c equal to ρ dA on the original smaller disk. Thus there is a smooth real P with dd^cP=β locally.

There is the following equivalence, with canonical representatives understood throughout. A function W on E is genuinely β-subharmonic if and only if its descended function w=W∘π⁻¹ satisfies the stipulated disk tests. The forward implication uses the lift F. On a small disk on which its image lies in a coordinate chart, W∘F+P∘F is the holomorphic composition of a subharmonic function, hence is subharmonic, unless it is identically −∞. Moreover dd^c(P∘F)=γ*h, so any other permitted smooth potential p_γ differs from P∘F by a harmonic function. This gives the required disk test. A constant disk at a pole has the permitted identically −∞ restriction, without assigning it a derivative. For the reverse implication, use disks obtained by composing normalization coordinate disks with π. The elementary composition property follows, for example, by regularizing a subharmonic function and applying the chain rule to its Laplacian, followed by the submean inequality. These arguments also preserve genuine upper values. In particular, the value of a subharmonic function is its limiting local area average, including value −∞; π is a homeomorphism, so the same canonical upper values descend. We never alter a representative on a null set.

2. Construction and estimates for the Green kernel.
In a Euclidean coordinate z=x+iy, direct computation gives
 dd^c v=(Δv/(4π))dx∧dy.
The flux of the gradient of log|z|² across a circle is 4π. Integration against a test function, followed by integration by parts on a punctured disk, therefore gives dd^c log|z|²=δ₀.

Choose a smooth cutoff supported in a normalization coordinate disk and equal to one near zero. The global locally integrable function G₁=χ log|z|² satisfies
 dd^cG₁=δ₀+α,
where α is a smooth real 2-form. Pairing with the constant test function gives ∫α=−1. The smooth form −β₀−α therefore has integral zero and has a smooth real periodic potential. Here is an explicit justification of this last assertion. For the dual lattice Λ*, expand a smooth mean-zero coefficient k in the characters exp(2πi ξ·z). The equation dd^cP=kβ₀ is solved, for ξ≠0, by
 P̂(ξ)=−k̂(ξ)/(π V|ξ|²),
and by P̂(0)=0. Repeated integration by parts gives rapid decay of the coefficients of k, so this series and every differentiated series converge. It produces a smooth real solution. Apply this construction to −β₀−α and add its solution to G₁. Subtracting the resulting finite mean gives G with
 dd^cG=δ₀−β₀,  ∫Gβ₀=0.
It is smooth away from zero and equals log|z|² plus a smooth real function near zero. Its canonical value there is −∞. The integral of |log|z||^r against r dr near zero is finite for every finite positive exponent, so G belongs to L^r for every finite r>0.

Let r∈L^p(E,β₀), p>1, and let p′=p/(p−1). Hölder's inequality, using translation invariance of β₀, proves that K(z)=∫G(z−t)r(t)β₀(t) is well-defined for every z and that
 ||K||∞≤||G||p′||r||p,
 |K(z+s)−K(z)|≤||r||p ||G(·+s)−G||p′.
The last norm tends to zero. One can see this directly by cutting off the logarithmic singularity to approximate G in L^p′ by smooth functions, whose translates converge uniformly. Hence K is bounded and uniformly continuous. Fubini's theorem is applicable in distributional pairings, since r and G are integrable and translations preserve their L¹ norms. It gives
 dd^cK=(r−∫rβ₀)β₀.
Also ∫Kβ₀=0. If r is smooth, change variables to write K(z)=∫G(t)r(z−t)β₀(t); derivatives can then be passed to r. Thus K is smooth, in particular when r is smooth and mean zero. This proves all asserted properties of the kernel and convolution, with the original normalization.

We will also use a direct consequence of the same Fourier computation: a distribution on E with dd^c equal to zero is constant. Its nonzero Fourier coefficients vanish because the Laplacian eigenvalues there are nonzero.

3. The reference and its descent.
The coefficient H−b is smooth and mean zero. Consequently Φ is smooth and dd^cΦ=(H−b)β₀. For Ψ=Φ+Σa_jG(·−q_j), addition of the kernel equations yields
 β+dd^cΨ=(H−A)β₀+Σa_jδ_qj=Mβ₀+Σa_jδ_qj.
This is positive because M>0. Near q_j all terms other than a_jG(·−q_j) are smooth, so in a normalization coordinate ζ,
 Ψ=a_j log|ζ|²+smooth.
It has genuine value −∞ there and is smooth and finite elsewhere.

To check genuineness without importing any solvability theorem, add a smooth local potential P for β. The locally integrable function Ψ+P has nonnegative distributional Laplacian. Regularization therefore has nonnegative Laplacian and satisfies the submean inequalities. Passing to the limit off the poles, and using the logarithmic limit −∞ at the poles, gives the genuine subharmonic representative Ψ+P. Thus Ψ is a genuine β-potential. Section 1 proves that ψ=Ψ∘π⁻¹ is a genuine h-potential with the claimed canonical values. This construction also applies when the pole list is empty.

4. All potentials in the ordinary class and their mass.
Let w∈C_ψ and W=w∘π. The disk tests make W+P subharmonic in every normalization coordinate. The two class inequalities imply that W is locally bounded on E\Q, that W(q_j)=−∞, and that
 W=a_j log|ζ|²+O(1)
near q_j. In particular W is locally integrable. Its distribution T_W=β+dd^cW is positive, and therefore is a positive Radon measure. On the compact torus, pairing dd^cW with 1 gives zero, so T_W(E)=H.

We check its point masses, rather than assuming that a bounded difference is harmless. The following elementary Jensen calculation fixes the normalization. If s is subharmonic near zero and μ=dd^cs, its circular average m(r) satisfies
 m(R)−m(r)=2∫_r^R μ(B_t)dt/t.
For smooth s this follows from the divergence theorem and dd^cs=Δs dA/(4π); convolution gives the same formula for a subharmonic s. Since μ(B_t) tends to μ({0}), taking logarithmic averages in this identity gives
 lim_{r→0} m(r)/log r²=μ({0}).
If s=a log|ζ|²+O(1), the limit is a. Apply this to s=W+P. The smooth background has no point mass, so T_W({q_j})=a_j, exactly.

The non-pluripolar measure in this situation can be read directly from its one-dimensional truncation definition. Locally use s=W+P and the measures 1_{s>−N}dd^c max(s,−N). On every relatively compact neighborhood in E\Q, s is bounded and for large N these measures equal dd^cs=T_W. At q_j the restriction factor excludes the point for every N. The resulting local measures therefore glue to
 ⟨β+dd^cW⟩=1_{E\Q}T_W.
This argument only uses local smooth potentials; it does not require the background to be a strictly positive form upstairs. Its mass is H−Σa_j=M. Pushforward by π proves the stated formula for MA_ext,h(w) and its finite mass M for every member of the entire class, with no regularity imposed on that member.

The prescribed measure ν=π_*(fβ₀) has mass F and is non-pluripolar. To check the latter, a relative pluripolar set on a locally irreducible curve pulls back, away from the finite singular set, to a locally polar set in normalization coordinates: pull back its local genuine plurisubharmonic defining function and apply the disk test. Such a non-identically −∞ subharmonic function is locally integrable, so its −∞ set has area zero. The finite inverse image of X_sing also has area zero. Thus every relative pluripolar set has zero fβ₀ mass upstairs and zero ν mass downstairs. This checks non-pluripolarity even when a density relative to h is unbounded.

5. Solving the equation.
Set c=M/F, which is positive. Then r=cf−M belongs to L^p and has mean zero. Section 2 gives a bounded continuous mean-zero v with dd^cv=(cf−M)β₀. Hence
 β+dd^cU=cfβ₀+Σa_jδ_qj,  U=Ψ+v.
This measure is positive. Off Q the function U is continuous; near a pole it is a_j log|ζ|² plus a bounded continuous function. The local regularization argument used for Ψ now proves that U is a genuine β-potential, including its prescribed value −∞ at each pole. Since v is bounded, U has the ordinary type of Ψ.

The function U is bounded above on the compact torus and is finite somewhere, so S=sup_E U is a finite real number. The descended u=(U−S)∘π⁻¹ is genuine by Section 1 and belongs to C_ψ. It is normalized by sup_Xu=0. The density cfβ₀ has no point masses, so the truncation calculation of Section 4 gives
 ⟨β+dd^cU⟩=cfβ₀.
It follows that MA_ext,h(u)=cν and cν(X)=M. Descent here is actual descent: all fibers of π are singletons and we have proved the disk tests and canonical values of the descended function. It is not an inference merely from a solution of a distributional equation upstairs.

6. Uniqueness, including initially rough competitors.
Suppose w∈C_ψ satisfies MA_ext,h(w)=dν with d>0. Its mass, already proved for every member of the class, is M. Consequently dF=M and d=c. Because π is a homeomorphism, equality of its pushforward Borel measures is equality of the original measures. Hence
 1_{E\Q}T_W=cfβ₀.
The only removed points are q_j, and Section 4 proves their masses are precisely a_j. We therefore recover the entire distributional measure:
 T_W=cfβ₀+Σa_jδ_qj=β+dd^cU.
Thus dd^c(W−U)=0. These functions are integrable, and the Fourier argument in Section 2 shows that W−U is a real constant almost everywhere. Equality upgrades to equality everywhere for the genuine representatives: after adding the same smooth local background potential, two subharmonic functions equal almost everywhere have the same limiting local averages and hence the same canonical values. This includes the common values −∞. Therefore w=u+K for a real constant K. If sup_Xw=0, then K=0. This establishes the asserted uniqueness throughout C_ψ, not just for continuous or smooth competitors.

7. Continuity and logarithmic disk coefficients.
On E\Q, U−S is real-valued and continuous. Near q_j it tends to −∞, because its logarithmic term has positive coefficient and its residual is bounded. The homeomorphism π therefore gives real continuity of u away from π(Q), and continuity into ℝ∪{−∞} with the order topology at every pole. In that topology, a neighborhood of −∞ contains an interval [−∞,B); precisely the proved logarithmic limit ensures its inverse image contains a neighborhood of the pole.

On E\Q, (U−S)−Ψ=v−S. Therefore the residual u−ψ, defined only off the common poles, extends to the continuous real function (v−S)∘π⁻¹ on X. This is an extension, not arithmetic with two infinite values. Section 6 proves the same conclusions for every solution, after adding its real constant.

For any nonconstant lifted disk meeting q_j at t₀, its local coordinate is ζ(F(t))=(t−t₀)^m g(t) with m≥1 and g holomorphic and nonvanishing. Consequently
 log|ζ(F(t))|²=m log|t−t₀|²+log|g(t)|²,
and the last term is smooth. The reference has coefficient ma_j on that disk. The solution has the same coefficient because its correction is bounded and continuous. All such restrictions are genuine subharmonic after adding the required disk potential, as proved in Section 1. Constant disks in the pole set retain the identically −∞ convention and have no assigned distributional derivative.

8. Resolutions, refinements, and measure normalization.
Let ρ:Y→X be a resolution in the usual sense of a proper bimeromorphic map from a smooth curve. Since Y is compact, the continuous map r=π⁻¹∘ρ is defined everywhere. The disk-lifting argument in Section 1, applied in coordinates on Y, proves it is holomorphic. It is generically biholomorphic. A nonconstant map between compact smooth curves has finite fibers and a positive local integer multiplicity at each fiber point, given by its first nonzero coordinate term. The sum of these multiplicities is locally constant in the target, by the argument principle on disjoint source coordinate disks, and thus constant on the connected target. Here the generic sum is one. Every fiber therefore has one point of multiplicity one, so r is biholomorphic. This proves ρ=π∘r. The identical argument applies to a smooth common refinement.

Under this biholomorphism the background is r*β=ρ*h, the genuine potential is W∘r, and local truncation measures and pole atoms transport by ordinary biholomorphic change of variables. In particular r_*⟨r*β+dd^c(W∘r)⟩=⟨β+dd^cW⟩. Pushing further to X gives exactly the same extended measure. Ordinary type inequalities, canonical values, and continuity also transport unchanged. There are no additional exceptional fibers or measure terms. This proves all the claimed independence statements.

Finally, π has generic degree one, not a degree determined by the vanishing of its differential at a cusp. The prescribed transformation is exactly ν=π_*(fβ₀). On the regular locus β=bβ₀ with b>0 and π biholomorphic, so ordinary change of variables gives
 ν=((f/b)∘π⁻¹)h.
The coefficient b includes the differential/Jacobian contribution in the pullback of the ambient form. This formula is asserted only on X_reg. The original measure and its pushforward give the finite singular set zero mass. There is no additional degree multiplier. All conclusions have been proved only for the explicitly stated dimension-one, torus-normalization family, finite logarithmic ordinary types with A<H, and normalization-side L^p data.

notes.summary: Complete scoped candidate using n1: an explicit projective curve with genus-one normalization and one unibranch cusp, not a projective cone. The normalization is an injective degree-one map from the square torus to P^4, h is restricted Fubini–Study, H=6 while the pullback degenerates at the cusp. A weight-one cusp type and positive nonconstant density give c=5, full-class uniqueness, proved descent, continuous residual and extended continuity at the pole. The bounded type gives real continuity everywhere as well.
notes.detailedSummary: On E=C/(Z+iZ), construct the elliptic function x=℘ by its convergent series and y=x'. The map π(z)=[1:x:y:x²:x³], extended at 0 to [0:0:0:0:1], is injective and immersive off 0; its image X is a reduced compact projective curve with one cusp. In the last affine chart, s=1/x and t=y/x³ satisfy t²=s³(4−g2s²−g3s³), analytically the ordinary cusp. Degree-two fiber counting for x proves the map's injectivity and regular immersion away from 0. The curve normalization is E, so it cannot be an irreducible one-dimensional projective cone, which would be a line. For h=FS restricted to X with dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, ∫Eπ*h=6 by the logarithmic pole of the Fubini–Study potential at 0. The pullback bβ0 vanishes like |z|² at 0; positivity is not assumed there. Choose the n1 reference with a single weight a=1 at the cusp, and ν=π_*[(1+(1/2)cos(2π Re z))β0]. Then F=1, M=5, c=5, and the residual correction is explicitly v=−(5/(2π))cos(2π Re z). By n1 the resulting normalized potential solves the equation in the entire prescribed ordinary type, all potentials in this type have mass 5, and all solutions differ by constants. The potential is extended-continuous with value −∞ at the cusp and the residual is real-continuous everywhere. With no poles the same curve also yields bounded-type solutions real-continuous on all of X. This gives a complete sufficient-condition package, expressly limited to dimension one, without claiming classification or new higher-dimensional theory.
notes.text:
EXPLICIT COMPACT NON-CONE EXAMPLE AND COMPLETE SCOPED SOLUTION PACKAGE

This note uses the fully proved sufficient-condition theorem in n1. It supplies an explicit compact example, checking rather than assuming its geometry, positivity properties, and normalization factors. Together the notes give a complete sufficient-condition answer scoped to dimension one.

1. Explicit torus functions, with the needed facts reconstructed.
Let Λ=Z+iZ and E=C/Λ, with β0=dx∧dy of total mass 1. Define
 x(z)=1/z²+Σ_{λ∈Λ\{0}}[(z−λ)^{-2}−λ^{-2}],
 y(z)=x'(z).
The series converges normally on compact subsets away from Λ: its summands are O(|λ|^{-3}) there, and this series converges on a two-dimensional lattice. Pairing λ and −λ proves x is even. The differentiated series for y is absolutely normally convergent and reindexing makes y periodic. Therefore x(z+ω)−x(z) is constant; for ω=1 or i, evaluation at z=−ω/2 and evenness make that constant zero. Thus x and y are meromorphic functions on E. At 0,
 x=z^{-2}+a_2 z²+a_4 z⁴+...,   y=−2z^{-3}+2a_2z+4a_4z³+... .
There are no other poles on E.

The elliptic function y²−4x³+g_2x+g_3 has no pole and has zero constant Laurent coefficient if g_2=20a_2 and g_3=28a_4. It is constant by the maximum principle on the compact torus and that constant is zero. Hence
 y²=4x³−g_2x−g_3.
For the square lattice g_3=0 also follows by the rotation of the defining lattice sums, but its value is immaterial here.

The meromorphic function x has degree two. Indeed the argument principle on a translated fundamental parallelogram gives two zeros, counted with multiplicity, of x−c for every finite c: opposite boundary integrals cancel, and its only pole has order two. This also proves the following elementary facts used in checking the embedding. A fiber of x consists of z and −z, counted with multiplicity. If x'(z)=0, its local multiplicity is exactly two and z=−z modulo Λ: otherwise z and −z would give at least four zeros. At such a point x''(z)≠0. Thus (x,y) is injective on E\{0}: equality of x gives w=z or −z, and equality of the odd function y either gives w=z or y=0, in which case −z=z. The map (x,y) is immersive there: if y≠0 use dx, and if y=0 use dy=x''dz. These arguments avoid reliance on a uniformization theorem or on an unchecked nonsingularity assertion for a cubic model.

2. The projective curve and its cusp.
Define
 π:E→P^4,   z↦[1:x(z):y(z):x(z)²:x(z)³]
away from 0, and set π(0)=[0:0:0:0:1]. The latter extension is holomorphic. In the last affine chart the coordinates are
 [s³,s²,t,s,1],   s=1/x=z²+O(z⁶),   t=y/x³=−2z³+O(z⁷).
The relation above becomes
 t²=s³(4−g_2s²−g_3s³).
The factor in parentheses is a nonvanishing analytic unit near s=0. Replacing t by t divided by its analytic square root makes the relation exactly t'^2=s³. If desired, take a normalization coordinate ζ satisfying s=ζ²; the parametrization is then t'=±ζ³. Hence the local image is the ordinary reduced irreducible cusp with local ring C{ζ²,ζ³}. Its normalization is C{ζ}, finite over the cusp ring (generated as module by 1 and ζ).

Away from 0, the first projective coordinate is nonzero, and the already proved properties of (x,y) make π injective and immersive. No such point maps to π(0). Therefore π is globally injective. Its image X is a compact reduced analytic curve: locally it is a smooth graph away from π(0), and the explicit analytic cusp above at π(0). Compactness and injectivity exclude unwanted additional local branches. Equivalently it is the projective closure of the affine algebraic graph given by y²=4x³−g_2x−g_3, the other coordinates x²,x³, so it is projective.

Thus X is connected, compact, reduced, of pure dimension one, locally irreducible and unibranch. It has exactly one singular point p=π(0). The map π is proper, finite, bijective and birational, with the local normalization just checked, so it is its normalization. In particular π is a homeomorphism. Its differential vanishes at 0; it is not an immersion there.

This curve is not a projective cone of the usual type mentioned in the question. A reduced irreducible projective cone of dimension one has a zero-dimensional reduced irreducible base, hence a single point, and is a projective line. Our curve has a cusp and its normalization is the genus-one torus E, not P^1. More intrinsically, no change of projective embedding turns this curve into such a cone. The example is also not an application of a log-terminal continuity theorem: the cusp is nonnormal, whereas that terminology requires normality.

3. Background, total mass, and the actual degeneracy.
Take h to be the restriction of the Fubini–Study form on P^4, using exactly
 dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂,
so its affine local potential is log(Σ|Z_j|²) after choosing a nonzero homogeneous coordinate. This is smooth and strictly positive in the ambient projective coordinate charts, as required by the local-embedding definition of h.

Set β=π*h=bβ0. It is smooth and positive off 0, but not positive at 0. In the last chart s=z²+..., t=−2z³+..., so the derivatives of all affine coordinate functions vanish at 0. Strict ambient positivity, with the leading derivative ds=2z dz+..., gives constants C_1,C_2>0 such that
 C_1|z|²≤b(z)≤C_2|z|²
for z near 0. In particular b(0)=0. This degeneracy is part of the example, not overlooked by a positivity assertion.

The total background mass is H=6 with the stated dd^c convention. To check it directly, on E\{0} write
 L(z)=log(1+|x|²+|y|²+|x|⁴+|x|⁶).
Then dd^cL=β there. The last-chart formula and x=z^{-2}+... show
 L=−6 log|z|²+smooth
near 0; the smooth term is the last-chart Fubini–Study potential plus a smooth change of local trivialization. Thus globally as distributions
 dd^cL=β−6δ0.
Pairing with 1 on E gives ∫Eβ=6. This independently checks the curvature normalization and the integer 6; it is not inferred from an unspecified convention for degree. The full map π has generic degree one, even though x alone has degree two.

4. Concrete nonconstant data and a genuine singularity type.
Apply n1 with one pole q=0 of weight a=1. Let G be its explicitly constructed mean-zero Green function and put
 Φ=G*((6−b)β0),   Ψ=Φ+G.
Then
 β+dd^cΨ=5β0+δ0.
Descend Ψ to the genuine reference ψ on X. Its actual ordinary singularity type is weight-one logarithmic type at the cusp: on the normalization it is log|z|²+smooth, with canonical value −∞ at 0. It has no other poles. The class is exactly all genuine h-potentials satisfying the two bounded-shift inequalities against ψ; rough potentials are included.

Choose
 f(z)=1+(1/2)cos(2π Re z),   ν=π_*(fβ0).
This is an everywhere positive smooth normalization density, with F=1. The measure downstairs has no atom at the cusp and is non-pluripolar. Near the cusp its density relative to h on the regular locus is f/b, which grows like |z|^{-2}; no bounded-density hypothesis with respect to h is being smuggled in.

The proportionality constant required by the original equation is
 c=(H−a)/F=5.
The correction in n1 is particularly explicit. Since β0=dx∧dy on this unit square torus,
 dd^c cos(2πx)=−π cos(2πx)β0.
Consequently
 v(z)=−(5/(2π))cos(2π Re z)
satisfies dd^cv=(5f−5)β0 and has mean zero; it is exactly the Green convolution correction. Therefore
 U=Ψ+v,   β+dd^cU=5fβ0+δ0.
Let S=sup_E U and set u=(U−S)∘π^{-1}. By the fully proved descent and measure arguments of n1,
 sup_Xu=0,   MA_ext,h(u)=5ν,
and its extended mass is 5, not 6. The omitted mass is the pole atom of weight one; this number uses dd^c log|z|²=δ0, not a different logarithmic convention.

All genuine potentials in this entire ordinary type have mass 5. Any genuine solution in this class, even with an initially unknown positive c and without a continuity assumption, has c=5 and equals u up to a constant. Supremum normalization makes it u. Thus this is not merely uniqueness among smooth normalization-side solutions.

The potential u is real-continuous on X\{p}. It tends to −∞ at p and is continuous as an extended real-valued function there. The residual, defined away from p by u−ψ, is the descended continuous real function v−S on all of X. We never define −∞−(−∞). Ambient smoothness downstairs at the cusp is not claimed. The construction and uniqueness force the same continuity for every solution in the type.

For an everywhere finite variant, take the empty pole list in n1 on this SAME singular curve. Then ψ=Φ is bounded and the specified ordinary type is the full bounded class. With the same f one obtains c=6 and the correction v=−(3/π)cos(2π Re z); the potential itself, not just a residual, is real-continuous everywhere downstairs. Thus the example family covers both bounded potentials and a nontrivial pole type.

5. Complete-result statement and limitations.
The sufficient hypotheses are the geometric torus-normalization assumptions, arbitrary smooth local-embedding Hermitian h in dimension one, a finite logarithmic reference with total weight A<H, and prescribed ν=π_*(fβ0) with f≥0 in L^p, p>1 and positive integral. They yield finite mass of the whole type, existence, constant-difference uniqueness in the whole genuine type, canonical descent, and precisely stated continuity. The explicit nonnormal projective cusp above checks that this family is nonempty and lies beyond the projective-cone and log-terminal backgrounds. It also displays a pullback background with genuine degeneracy, which the proof compensates by a constructed smooth correction rather than treating it as positive.

All relevant measure transformations, background mass, lost pole mass, degree one, and local Jacobian behavior were checked above and in n1. All resolutions and common refinements are biholomorphic to the normalization, as proved in n1, so the statement has the required independence. No existence, uniqueness, descent, positivity of the degenerate pullback, or continuity conclusion is an assumption. No external nonlinear PDE or singular-space regularity theorem is imported; the elementary Green/Fourier proof and the elliptic-function example have been reconstructed. This completes the exact requested sufficient-condition package in the explicitly stated one-dimensional scope. It is not a classification of arbitrary unibranch singularities and makes no claim for n>1 or for arbitrary prescribed singularity classes.

correctness.report:
The new reasoning checks out, with the equation and full-class conclusions using the declared support n1, whose hypotheses are verified here. Normal convergence and periodicity of the elliptic-function series are correctly established. The order-two pole of x gives its degree-two fiber count; parity and the derivative argument then establish injectivity and immersion of (x,y) away from 0.

In the last projective chart, the coordinates satisfy the stated cusp equation. Dividing by an analytic square root of its unit factor gives t'^2=s³, with normalization parameter ζ and local ring C{ζ²,ζ³}. Together with compact injectivity and immersion elsewhere, this establishes the reduced unibranch curve, its finite bijective torus normalization, and its unique singular point. An irreducible one-dimensional projective cone is a line, so this cuspidal curve is not such a cone.

The background calculation correctly gives b comparable to |z|² near the cusp. The global locally integrable Fubini–Study potential has singular part −6 log|z|², hence dd^c L=β−6δ0 and H=6. The normalization map has generic degree one; the degree two of x introduces no measure factor. For the specified data, F=1, removed pole mass is 1, and c=5. The correction −5/(2π) cos(2π Re z) has exactly the required dd^c. The bounded variant likewise has c=6 and the stated correction.

The summaries accurately preserve dependence on n1, full ordinary-class uniqueness, residual versus potential continuity, degeneration, and the dimension-one limitation. No additional unresolved nonroutine external premise is required.

The correction only clarifies that “genus-one” refers to the normalization.

reconstruction.report: Using the proved supporting note n1, all application hypotheses are verified. The series construction, degree-two fibers of x, and cusp coordinates establish the claimed finite bijective genus-one normalization and non-cone geometry. The independent reconstruction also verifies projectivity directly. The pullback Fubini–Study background genuinely degenerates like |z|², while its total mass is exactly six in the stipulated normalization. The chosen density has integral one; the pole type therefore gives c=5 and the displayed correction, whereas the bounded variant gives c=6. Full-class uniqueness, canonical descent, the precise continuity statements, and refinement independence follow legitimately from n1. The extracted statement and both summaries preserve these claims and their limitations.
reconstruction.statement:
Explicit nonnormal, non-cone compact example satisfying the sufficient-condition theorem of supporting note w7-1/n1.

Use dd^c=(i/(2π))∂∂̄. Let Λ=ℤ+iℤ, E=ℂ/Λ, and β₀=dx∧dy, of total mass one. Define
 x(z)=1/z²+Σ_{λ∈Λ∖{0}}[(z−λ)⁻²−λ⁻²],   y(z)=x′(z).
The series converges normally on compact subsets of ℂ∖Λ. The functions x and y are meromorphic and Λ-periodic, x is even, and y is odd. Their only pole on E is at 0. Their Laurent expansions there are
 x=z⁻²+a₂z²+a₄z⁴+⋯,
 y=−2z⁻³+2a₂z+4a₄z³+⋯.
Set g₂=20a₂ and g₃=28a₄. They satisfy
 y²=4x³−g₂x−g₃,
and g₃=0 for this square lattice.

The meromorphic map x:E→ℙ¹ has degree two: for every finite c, x−c has exactly two zeros counted with multiplicity. Its fibers consist of z and −z, counted with multiplicity. If x′(z)=0 at z≠0, then the local multiplicity is exactly two, z=−z modulo Λ, and x″(z)≠0. The map (x,y) is injective and immersive on E∖{0}.

Define π:E→ℙ⁴ by
 π(z)=[1:x(z):y(z):x(z)²:x(z)³]   for z≠0,
 π(0)=[0:0:0:0:1].
This extension is holomorphic. In the last affine chart its coordinates are
 [s³,s²,t,s,1],   s=1/x=z²+O(z⁶),   t=y/x³=−2z³+O(z⁷),
and
 t²=s³(4−g₂s²−g₃s³).
The factor 4−g₂s²−g₃s³ is an analytic unit near s=0. With t′=t/(4−g₂s²−g₃s³)^{1/2}, the local relation is t′²=s³. There is a local normalization coordinate ζ with s=ζ² and t′=±ζ³. Thus the local image at π(0) is the ordinary reduced irreducible cusp, with local ring ℂ{ζ²,ζ³} and normalization ℂ{ζ}; the normalization ring is finite over the cusp ring and is generated as a module by 1 and ζ.

The map π is globally injective and immersive away from 0. Its image X is a connected compact reduced projective analytic curve of pure dimension one, locally irreducible and unibranch, with exactly one singular point p=π(0). It is the projective closure of the affine graph determined by y²=4x³−g₂x−g₃ and the additional coordinates x²,x³. The map π:E→X is proper, finite, bijective, birational, and is the normalization of X; it is a homeomorphism. Its differential vanishes at 0. Its generic degree is one, although x alone has degree two.

The curve X is not a reduced irreducible one-dimensional projective cone of the usual type: such a cone over a reduced irreducible zero-dimensional base is a projective line, whereas X has a cusp and genus-one normalization E rather than ℙ¹. No projective re-embedding makes X such a cone. The cusp is nonnormal, so the example lies outside the usual log-terminal hypotheses requiring normality. This X satisfies the geometric hypotheses of w7-1/n1; that theorem applies to every background, finite logarithmic ordinary type, and normalization-side density satisfying its stated hypotheses.

For the following concrete data, let h be the restriction to X of the Fubini–Study form on ℙ⁴ with the stated dd^c normalization. In a projective affine chart its local potential is log(Σ_j|Z_j|²) after setting a nonzero homogeneous coordinate equal to one. This gives a smooth strictly positive ambient form, so h satisfies the local-embedding Hermitian requirement. Write β=π*h=bβ₀. Then b is smooth, positive on E∖{0}, and b(0)=0. There exist C₁,C₂>0 and a neighborhood of 0 such that
 C₁|z|²≤b(z)≤C₂|z|².
In particular the pullback background is genuinely degenerate at the cusp.

The total background mass is H=∫_E β=6 in the original normalization. More explicitly, on E∖{0}, let
 L(z)=log(1+|x|²+|y|²+|x|⁴+|x|⁶).
Then dd^cL=β there, L=−6 log|z|² plus a smooth function near 0, and globally as distributions
 dd^cL=β−6δ₀.

Let G be the mean-zero periodic Green function of w7-1/n1, with dd^cG=δ₀−β₀ and G=log|z|² plus a smooth function near 0. Choose the single pole q=0 of weight a=1, and define
 Φ=G*((6−b)β₀),   Ψ=Φ+G,   ψ=Ψ∘π⁻¹.
Then ψ is a genuine h-potential and
 β+dd^cΨ=5β₀+δ₀.
Its ordinary singularity class consists of all genuine h-potentials w for which there is a finite C with w≤ψ+C and ψ≤w+C, using canonical extended values. This includes rough potentials. On the normalization the reference is log|z|² plus a smooth function at 0, has canonical value −∞ there, and has no other poles.

Choose the positive nonconstant smooth density
 f(z)=1+(1/2)cos(2π Re z),   ν=π_*(fβ₀).
It has F=∫_E fβ₀=1. The measure ν is finite, positive, non-pluripolar, and has no atom at p. On X_reg its density relative to h is (f/b)∘π⁻¹; near the cusp this density grows like |z|⁻². No bounded-density assertion relative to h is made, and no additional degree factor occurs in the pushforward.

For this singularity class and these data, the proportionality constant is c=(H−a)/F=5. The correction is explicitly
 v(z)=−(5/(2π))cos(2π Re z).
Indeed the relevant identities are
 dd^c cos(2π Re z)=−π cos(2π Re z)β₀,
 dd^cv=(5f−5)β₀,
and v is the mean-zero Green convolution correction. Define
 U=Ψ+v,   S=sup_E U,   u=(U−S)∘π⁻¹.
Then S is finite, u descends as a genuine h-potential in the specified ordinary type, and
 β+dd^cU=5fβ₀+δ₀,
 ⟨β+dd^cU⟩=5fβ₀,
 sup_X u=0,   MA_ext,h(u)=5ν.
The extended non-pluripolar mass is five, while the total distributional background mass is six; the omitted pole atom has weight one with dd^c log|z|²=δ₀.

Every genuine h-potential in this entire ordinary type has extended non-pluripolar mass five. If any such potential w satisfies MA_ext,h(w)=dν for some d>0, then d=5 and w=u+K for a real constant K, with equality of canonical extended values. Thus the normalized solution is unique among all genuine potentials in the type, not merely smooth normalization-side solutions.

The potential u is real-continuous on X∖{p}, tends to −∞ at p, and is continuous there as a function into ℝ∪{−∞} with the order topology. The residual u−ψ on X∖{p} extends to the continuous real-valued function (v−S)∘π⁻¹ on all of X. This residual is not defined by subtracting −∞ from −∞ at p. Every solution in this type has the same continuity properties up to an additive constant. Ambient smoothness downstairs at the cusp is not asserted.

An everywhere finite variant on the same singular curve uses the empty pole list. Its reference is ψ₀=Φ∘π⁻¹, and its ordinary type is the entire class of bounded genuine h-potentials. For the same f and ν, define
 v₀(z)=−(3/π)cos(2π Re z),
 U₀=Φ+v₀,   S₀=sup_E U₀,   u₀=(U₀−S₀)∘π⁻¹.
Then β+dd^cU₀=6fβ₀, sup_X u₀=0, and MA_ext,h(u₀)=6ν. Every member of the bounded type has extended mass six. Every solution in this type with an initially unspecified positive proportionality constant has constant six and differs from u₀ by a real constant. The normalized solution u₀ itself is real-continuous everywhere on X, including p.

All resolutions and smooth common refinements of X are biholomorphic to its normalization E, with their maps to X factoring through π. Hence the asserted equations, singularity classes, measures, canonical descent, and continuity statements are resolution- and refinement-independent. The sufficient-condition conclusions remain scoped to the dimension-one family of w7-1/n1; no assertion is made for arbitrary higher-dimensional unibranch spaces or arbitrary prescribed singularity types.
reconstruction.proof:
We first reconstruct the example and all its geometric and numerical features, and then apply the proved supporting theorem w7-1/n1 after checking every hypothesis.

1. The elliptic functions from their series.
On a compact subset avoiding Λ, the summand (z−λ)⁻²−λ⁻² is O(|λ|⁻³), uniformly for large λ. The two-dimensional lattice sum of |λ|⁻³ converges. This proves normal convergence of the displayed series. Its derivative is
 y(z)=−2 Σ_{λ∈Λ}(z−λ)⁻³,
which also converges normally away from Λ. Reindexing this absolutely convergent series proves that y is Λ-periodic. Reindexing the original series by λ↦−λ proves that x is even; hence y is odd. Since x′ is periodic, x(z+ω)−x(z) is constant for each lattice generator ω=1,i. Evaluate at z=−ω/2, where neither side has a pole. Evenness gives this constant as zero. Thus x is periodic as well and both functions descend meromorphically to E.

Expanding (z−λ)⁻² near zero and pairing λ with −λ gives
 x=z⁻²+a₂z²+a₄z⁴+⋯,
 y=−2z⁻³+2a₂z+4a₄z³+⋯.
There is no constant term, by the subtraction in the series, and no odd powers. Their only pole on E is zero.

The Laurent principal and constant terms of y²−4x³ are −20a₂z⁻²−28a₄. Hence
 y²−4x³+20a₂x+28a₄
has no poles. A holomorphic function on the compact torus is constant, and its expansion at zero has constant term zero. It is therefore identically zero. This proves the relation with g₂=20a₂ and g₃=28a₄. The invariance iΛ=Λ gives directly from the series x(iz)=−x(z). Comparing its z⁴ coefficient proves a₄=0, so g₃=0 for this lattice.

2. Degree, fibers, and immersion.
For finite c, the elliptic function x−c has one pole of order two on E. Integrate its logarithmic derivative around a translated fundamental parallelogram whose boundary avoids its zeros and pole. Opposite sides cancel by periodicity. The argument principle therefore gives exactly two zeros counted with multiplicity. In particular x:E→ℙ¹ has degree two and is surjective. Evenness gives the two points z and −z in each finite fiber, with multiplicity when they coincide.

If y(z)=x′(z)=0 at z≠0, then x−x(z) has multiplicity at least two there. Unless z=−z modulo Λ, the distinct point −z gives another zero, contradicting total multiplicity two. Thus z is a nonzero point of order two. Conversely, at any such point evenness and periodicity imply x(z+u)=x(z−u), so the multiplicity is at least two. It is exactly two by the zero count, and x″(z)≠0.

It follows that (x,y) is injective on E\{0}. Indeed x determines the pair z,−z; when they are distinct y is nonzero and its opposite signs separate them. If y is zero, the two points are the same. It is also immersive: if y≠0, dx≠0; if y=0, dy=x″(z)dz≠0.

For later use, the affine cubic C given by y²=4x³−g₂x−g₃ is exactly the image of this pair. For every finite x-value, the two preimages give both square-root y-values, or the single value zero. The cubic is smooth. At a point with y≠0 its derivative in y is nonzero. At a point with y=0, differentiate the elliptic identity and cancel y first on its nonzero locus to obtain
 2y′=12x²−g₂
identically, by holomorphic continuation. Here y′=x″≠0, so the derivative of the cubic polynomial in x is nonzero. Thus (x,y):E\{0}→C is a bijective local biholomorphism.

3. Projective extension and the cusp.
Near zero, multiply the homogeneous coordinates [1:x:y:x²:x³] by z⁶. All resulting coordinates are holomorphic and the last has value one at zero. This proves that the stated extension is holomorphic and takes zero to p=[0:0:0:0:1]. Its last-chart coordinates are
 (s³,s²,t,s),  s=1/x=z²+O(z⁶),  t=y/x³=−2z³+O(z⁷).
The elliptic identity gives
 t²=s³(4−g₂s²−g₃s³).
The factor in parentheses is a holomorphic unit with value four. Choose a local square root with value two and set t′=t/(4−g₂s²−g₃s³)^(1/2). Then t′²=s³. Write s=z²u(z), u(0)=1, choose its square root, and set ζ=z u(z)^(1/2). This is an invertible normalization coordinate. It gives s=ζ² and t′=−ζ³ for this choice of square root; changing the choice changes the sign. These parametrizations fill the germ t′²=s³.

For completeness, the local ring assertion follows without an appeal to a classification of singularities. Division by the monic polynomial t′²−s³ leaves a convergent series A(s)+t′B(s). Its substitution at s=ζ²,t′=−ζ³ is A(ζ²)−ζ³B(ζ²). The even and odd parts show that this vanishes only when both A and B vanish. The kernel of the parametrization is therefore exactly (t′²−s³), and its image ring is ℂ{ζ²,ζ³}. It is a domain, so the cusp is reduced and irreducible. Its fraction field contains ζ=−t′/s. The element ζ is integral since ζ²=s, and ℂ{ζ} is generated over the cusp ring by 1 and ζ: split any convergent series into its even and odd powers. A meromorphic germ integral over the cusp ring cannot have negative order, since in a monic integral equation its highest power would then have strictly smallest order. It is consequently holomorphic. This proves that ℂ{ζ} is precisely the integral closure, and verifies the finite normalization and nonnormality assertions.

The global image can also be identified explicitly without invoking a proper-image or algebraization theorem. In homogeneous coordinates Z₀,…,Z₄ take the reduced projective locus given by
 Z₁²=Z₀Z₃,
 Z₁Z₃=Z₀Z₄,
 Z₃²=Z₁Z₄,
 Z₂²=4Z₀Z₄−g₂Z₀Z₁−g₃Z₀².
On Z₀≠0 these equations give the affine cubic graph with extra coordinates x² and x³, already identified with the image of E\{0}. On Z₀=0 they force Z₁=Z₃=Z₂=0, leaving only p. In the chart Z₄=1, write a=Z₀, b=Z₁, t=Z₂, s=Z₃. The equations reduce to b=s², a=s³ and the cusp equation above. Thus this reduced projective locus is exactly π(E), is smooth away from p, and has the ordinary cusp at p. It is the projective closure of the stated affine graph.

The affine cubic is irreducible: as a monic quadratic in y, a factorization would require the degree-three polynomial 4x³−g₂x−g₃ to be a square polynomial, which it is not. Its projective closure is therefore irreducible and has pure dimension one. Alternatively, its dense affine part is the connected smooth image of E\{0}, and the only added point is p. The local descriptions prove reducedness and local irreducibility everywhere. Hence X is connected, compact, reduced, unibranch, and has exactly one singular point.

The map π is globally injective: its finite points lie in Z₀≠0 and are separated by (x,y), while zero maps to p. It is an immersion away from zero by Section 2, and its affine-coordinate derivatives at zero all vanish by the displayed expansions. It is proper because E is compact. On the affine part it is biholomorphic, and at p it is the finite normalization just proved. Thus it is finite, bijective, birational, and the normalization of X. It is a homeomorphism by compactness. Its generic degree is one. The degree-two statement about x alone is a different map and must not be attached to π.

A reduced irreducible projective cone of dimension one in the usual sense has a reduced irreducible zero-dimensional base, hence a single point; its cone is a projective line. Our curve has a cusp and therefore is not such a line. Its normalization is also E rather than ℙ¹: dz is a nonzero holomorphic one-form on E, whereas a holomorphic form on ℙ¹ would be f(z)dz with f entire and f(z)=O(|z|⁻²) at infinity, forcing f=0. These intrinsic properties persist under re-embedding. The cusp ring is not normal, as the integral element ζ above is missing from it, so this example is outside the usual log-terminal hypotheses requiring normality.

4. Background and its exact total mass.
The Fubini–Study form in the stipulated normalization is dd^c log(1+Σ|w_j|²) in an affine chart. Its Hermitian matrix is a positive multiple of
 ((1+|w|²)I−w*⊗w)/(1+|w|²)².
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality makes this matrix strictly positive. Chart potentials differ by logarithms of squared moduli of nonvanishing holomorphic functions, so their dd^c forms agree. Consequently its restriction h to X is a smooth strictly positive ambient background in the required local-embedding sense.

The pullback β=bβ₀ is smooth. It is positive on E\{0} because π is immersive there. At zero the differential vanishes, so b(0)=0. More precisely, in the last affine chart the coordinate map is (s³,s²,t,s). Its derivative has s′=2z+O(z⁵), t′=−6z²+O(z⁶), and derivatives of s² and s³ of higher order. Its Euclidean squared norm is therefore comparable to |z|². The smooth positive ambient metric is uniformly comparable to the Euclidean metric in a small chart. Since β₀=dx∧dy for this lattice, this proves constants C₁,C₂>0 with
 C₁|z|²≤b(z)≤C₂|z|²
near zero. Thus the degeneracy is real, not suppressed in the construction.

On E\{0}, the function
 L=log(1+|x|²+|y|²+|x|⁴+|x|⁶)
has dd^cL=β. Near zero let F=(z⁶,z⁶x,z⁶y,z⁶x²,z⁶x³), a holomorphic vector with nonzero last component. Then
 L=−6 log|z|²+log||F||².
The second summand is smooth and its dd^c is β near zero. The identity dd^c log|z|²=δ₀ thus gives globally
 dd^cL=β−6δ₀.
The function L is locally integrable on the compact torus. Pairing its derivative with 1 proves H=∫β=6, with precisely the original normalization and no degree correction.

5. Application to the pole class and concrete density.
We now check all hypotheses of w7-1/n1. The lattice is ℤ+iℤ, whose Euclidean fundamental area is one; hence β₀=dx∧dy. Sections 2–3 give finite bijective torus normalization, biholomorphic off one point, and all the required properties of X. Section 4 gives the required smooth ambient background, with H=6 and possibly degenerate pullback. Choose q=0 and a=1; then A=1<H and M=5. The theorem therefore constructs the smooth Φ=G*((6−b)β₀), the genuine reference Ψ=Φ+G, and its genuine descent ψ, with
 β+dd^cΨ=5β₀+δ₀.
Near zero Ψ=log|z|² plus a smooth function and its canonical value is −∞. Away from zero it is smooth. The ordinary class is precisely the class defined by the two extended-value inequalities in the question; no regularity restriction on its members has been added.

The prescribed f=1+(1/2)cos(2π Re z) is well-defined on this torus, smooth, nonconstant, and satisfies 1/2≤f≤3/2. Thus f belongs, for example, to L²(E,β₀), and its mean is F=1. The supporting theorem applies with p=2. It gives a finite positive non-pluripolar measure ν=π_*(fβ₀), with no atom at p. On X_reg its density relative to h is (f/b)∘π⁻¹. Since f is bounded above and below by positive constants and b is comparable to |z|², this density is comparable to |z|⁻² near the cusp. This observation does not claim boundedness with respect to h and does not change the normalization-side L² condition. The pushforward has no degree multiplier: π has generic degree one, and the full Jacobian behavior is already in b.

The required proportionality constant is c=M/F=5. The differential normalization gives, by Δ cos(2πx)=−4π² cos(2πx),
 dd^c cos(2π Re z)=−π cos(2π Re z)β₀.
Consequently
 v=−(5/(2π))cos(2π Re z)
has mean zero and satisfies dd^cv=(5f−5)β₀. It is exactly the Green convolution correction, because that correction also has mean zero and the same derivative, and a harmonic distribution on the torus is constant, as proved in w7-1/n1.

Set U=Ψ+v, S=sup_EU, and u=(U−S)∘π⁻¹. The supporting theorem gives S finite, genuine descent in the stated ordinary class, and sup_Xu=0. Direct addition also verifies
 β+dd^cU=5fβ₀+δ₀.
Deleting the pole atom in the one-dimensional non-pluripolar product gives ⟨β+dd^cU⟩=5fβ₀ and MA_ext,h(u)=5ν. Its extended mass is five; its full positive distributional measure has mass six. The removed atom has weight one, not a coefficient differing by 2 or π, since dd^c log|z|²=δ₀.

The theorem proves, for every genuine potential in this entire ordinary class, extended mass five. It also proves that any such w with MA_ext,h(w)=dν and d>0 has d=5 and w=u+K for a real constant, everywhere with canonical extended values. Thus the normalized solution is unique even among initially rough competitors.

The same theorem gives real continuity of u on X\{p}, limit −∞ at p, and order-topology continuity at p. On X\{p}, u−ψ=(v−S)∘π⁻¹; this extends as a continuous finite function on all of X. It is an extension of the off-pole residual, not a definition using −∞−(−∞). Constant-difference uniqueness gives these conclusions for every solution in the class. None of these statements claims ambient smoothness at the cusp.

6. The everywhere finite variant.
Use the empty pole list. Then M=H=6, the reference on E is the same smooth Φ, and ψ₀=Φ∘π⁻¹ is bounded and continuous on X. The two ordinary-type inequalities against a bounded reference are equivalent to two-sided boundedness. Hence the specified type is exactly the entire class of bounded genuine h-potentials, without any imposed continuity condition on competitors.

The same f has F=1, so c=6. The explicit mean-zero correction is
 v₀=−(3/π)cos(2π Re z),
for dd^cv₀=3cos(2π Re z)β₀=(6f−6)β₀. Define U₀=Φ+v₀, S₀=sup_EU₀, and u₀=(U₀−S₀)∘π⁻¹. The supporting theorem, or direct addition of these derivatives followed by its descent argument, gives
 β+dd^cU₀=6fβ₀,  MA_ext,h(u₀)=6ν,  sup_Xu₀=0.
All bounded genuine potentials in this type have extended mass six. Every solution with an initially unspecified positive proportionality constant therefore has constant six and differs from u₀ by a real constant. Since Φ+v₀ is continuous and π is a homeomorphism, u₀ is a finite real-continuous function on all of X, including p.

7. Refinements and scope.
The resolution argument of w7-1/n1 applies to this X: every resolution and every smooth common refinement is biholomorphic to E over X. Pullbacks of the background, canonical potentials, and one-dimensional truncation measures transport by that biholomorphism and push to the same measures on X. Thus all equations, ordinary types, pole conventions, descent, and continuity assertions just obtained are resolution- and refinement-independent, with no exceptional correction or extra degree factor. This proves the claimed explicit nonnormal non-cone example and its two variants, within exactly the scoped dimension-one sufficient-condition family.
